values.value: Model Context Protocol turns your CMS into a place your AI assistant can actually work in — safely, through the same doors a human editor uses.
Model Context Protocol turns your CMS into a place your AI assistant can actually work in — through the same doors a human editor uses.

value.markup:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI assistants talk to applications through small, focused tool servers. Instead of screen-scraping a backoffice or hand-rolling a private API, an assistant gets a documented set of tools — create this, inspect that, publish the other — and the application stays in charge of validation, permissions and defaults.

That last part is the awesome bit. Every tool call goes through the application's own rules. You get the guardrails of the CMS and the reach of the assistant at the same time.
1. It's the same door. The assistant works through the management API with the same validation a human editor hits in the backoffice. No shadow copies, no side databases, nothing to reconcile later.
2. It's inspectable. Tools like get-document-type-by-id and get-property-value-template mean the assistant reads the real state before writing — fewer hallucinated shapes, fewer silent failures.
3. It's composable. Schema tools, content tools, media tools — small servers with small surfaces. Add what your workflow needs, ignore the rest.

values.value: The whole conversation, in colour. Photo: Chris Ried / Unsplash
Every agent that ever had to guess an API shape
Read the schema, then write the value. MCP makes that order the natural one.

value.markup: And when something is rejected, the error tells you what to fix. That feedback loop — try, read, adjust — is exactly the loop MCP was designed for.

values.value: Two MCP servers, one backoffice: how schema work and content work split cleanly across the umbraco and umbraco-editor tools — and why that separation is the point.
Two servers, one backoffice — how the schema/content split makes agentic CMS work clean.

value.markup:
This site runs on two MCP servers. The umbraco server owns the schema: document types, element types, data types, templates, media types, domains. The umbraco-editor server owns the content: pages, blocks, publishing. One is the architect; the other is the editor.

The split matters because it mirrors how a real team works. Schema changes are deliberate and rare; content changes are constant and safe. Putting them behind separate tool surfaces keeps the risky operations visible and the routine ones frictionless.

values.value: Everything connects. Photo: Alina Grubnyak / Unsplash
Schema tools for the architect, content tools for the editor — and neither has to pretend to be the other.

value.markup: And when the two meet in the middle — a block grid configured by one server, filled with content by the other — you get exactly what you're reading: a site whose every layer was built over MCP, verified by reading back what actually landed.
